stem: A transplant candidate with strong family history of malignancy asks about post-transplant cancer screening. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: More aggressive screening tests and/or more frequent screening intervals may be required
Family history never influences post-transplant cancer screening
Cancer screening is unnecessary after transplantation
Only one lifetime screening test is ever needed regardless of risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines is a minimum standard, but more aggressive screening tests and/or more frequent intervals may be required based on family history, personal history, post-transplant course, and current medical status.

rationale_incorrect.B: Family history is among factors that may require more aggressive or frequent screening.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recommended cancer screening continues after transplantation with possible intensification when indicated.
rationale_incorrect.D: Screening intervals may be individualized rather than limited to a single lifetime test.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer → 5.a.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: more aggressive screening tests and/or more frequent screening intervals may be required

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 5.a. (more aggressive/frequent screening when indicated); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Individualized cancer-screening intensity angle distinct from malignancy-prevention combo (cctc-3116) and hepatitis B HCC prevention (cctc-1112); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.

stem: When counseling transplant candidates about long-term malignancy surveillance, which screening-guideline statement aligns with standard references?

options.text: Posttransplant cancer-screening guidelines developed for renal transplant recipients are applicable to most transplant recipients
Cancer screening applies only to kidney recipients and never to other organ recipients
No cancer screening is recommended after transplantation
Screening guidelines are identical for every recipient regardless of organ type or risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Posttransplant cancer-screening guidelines developed for renal transplant recipients are applicable to most transplant recipients, with individualized adjustments when indicated.

rationale_incorrect.B: Renal-derived screening guidelines are described as applicable to most transplant recipients rather than kidney recipients alone.
rationale_incorrect.C: Routine cancer screening is recommended after transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Screening may be individualized based on history and course rather than being identical for every recipient.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer → 5.b.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Posttransplant cancer–screening guidelines have been developed for renal transplant recipients and are applicable to most transplant recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 5.b. (renal-derived screening guidelines applicable to most recipients); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Cross-organ screening-guideline applicability angle distinct from individualized screening intensity (cctc-2149) and ACS minimum-standard item (cctc-2151); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.

stem: During pretransplant evaluation teaching about malignancy prevention, which baseline screening principle aligns with standard references?

options.text: Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines as minimum standards
No routine cancer screening is recommended for transplant candidates or recipients
Cancer screening is deferred until ten years after every transplant
Only skin examination is ever required with no other screening

explanation.rationale_correct: Cancer prevention includes routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines as minimum standards, with more aggressive screening when family history, personal history, or post-transplant course warrants it.

rationale_incorrect.B: Routine ACS-guided screening is recommended rather than omitted.
rationale_incorrect.C: Screening begins as part of health maintenance rather than being universally deferred for a decade.
rationale_incorrect.D: Multiple screening modalities are addressed rather than skin examination alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer → 5.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 5. (routine ACS cancer screening as minimum guidelines); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. ACS minimum-screening standard angle distinct from renal-guideline applicability (cctc-2150) and individualized interval counseling (cctc-2149); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.

stem: A coordinator is updating malignancy-screening teaching for the evaluation team. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: More aggressive screening tests or more frequent intervals may be required based on family or personal history.
American Cancer Society guidelines represent minimum screening standards.
Cancer screening is never needed after transplantation.
Renal transplant cancer-screening guidelines are applicable to most transplant recipients.

explanation.rationale_correct: Individualized screening intensity, ACS minimum standards, and applicability of renal-derived guidelines to most recipients are supported. Statement III is false because routine cancer screening is recommended after transplantation.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—renal transplant screening guidelines apply to most recipients.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement III is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false because cancer screening is part of post-transplant health maintenance.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer → 5.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: more aggressive screening tests and/or more frequent screening intervals … Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines … applicable to most transplant recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 5.a.–b. (individualized screening, ACS minimum, renal guidelines for most recipients); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Cancer-screening combo distinct from malignancy-prevention combo (cctc-3116) and PTLD presentation combo (cctc-2148); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.
